title: Three Months of Challenge in the United States and Canada
paragraphs: It was after the selection was finished and my destination had been decided that Duke University, with which the agreement should have ended last year, sent out a renewed call with the condition "only one student for one month." Both we students and the professors were puzzled by this unusual situation, but I sincerely thank the many people whose support made it possible for me to accomplish this fruitful study abroad. I observed for one week in breast oncology at MD Anderson Cancer Center, then did four weeks in pediatric hematology/oncology at Duke University and four weeks of basic research in the laboratory of Dr. 松波宏明, and finally did a four-week clerkship in the emergency department at McGill University in Canada. In addition, by being selected as a fourth-term student of "Tobitate! Study Abroad JAPAN," I gained not only funding but also many fellow exchange students from different fields, and through many discoveries and diverse viewpoints I was able to lead a very full study abroad life.

[Life at Duke] For me, Duke University was a place that accepted my hungry self and let me grow as a person and mentally. The advance procedures were tremendously complicated, such as the visa, remittance of tuition, obtaining BLS, a urine test in Yokohama, and nearly 15 kinds of online training, and I nearly lost heart many times. But for that very reason a rebellious spirit worked in me, to show performance on site worth that cost, and although there were situations in which I shed tears every week, I think I was able to realize the clerkship I had wanted. At Duke I did my clerkship in pediatric hematology/oncology. I had also experienced pediatric oncology in the clinical clerkships at Nagoya University, but I felt big differences between Japan and the United States. First, the patients' hospital stays are very short. In Japan, treating leukemia requires parent and child to devote their lives to hospital stays lasting many months, and a harsh reality awaits both mother and child. In the United States, however, even during chemotherapy, patients are admitted only for treatments that require hospitalization (such as 48 hours of continuous infusion to avoid renal damage), so they are discharged in a few days and the course of treatment is to come back two weeks later for a few days in hospital again. Second, because there are many African-Americans in North Carolina, one third of the patients were admitted for sickle cell crisis. This is acute pain occurring in patients with sickle cell disease, and apparently the sickle-shaped cells clog narrow blood vessels because of their shape, causing pain. From the age of kindergarten onward the patient is asked "how much does it hurt," and discharge is often decided by that scale, so some patients kept answering 8 or 10, for reasons such as not wanting to go to school or wanting to keep their parents' attention. What stayed with me was talking with the attending that "we have to start by educating the parents." Looking back on the clerkship, what I made efforts at was putting a load on myself every week and being conscious of asserting my own thoughts and working on them. At the start of the clerkship I was to "observe" the outpatient clinic. Because it was so lonely and painful that I could not stand it, I asserted to the attending, "I did not come as an observer!" and was able to change my clerkship to inpatients. And on the last day of the first week, with guidance from a resident, I somehow managed to present a patient by reading the script word for word. In the second week my presentation skills improved, and not only could I present with just notes, with some ad-libbing, but I also tried writing charts, did history taking and physical examination alone, and gave a talk on a disease (pediatric ITP) including the latest findings. In the third week not only was my assignment increased to two patients, but I became able to give my own opinion on the treatment plan. I was also asked by the resident to "go ask the patient about such and such," and I was glad, feeling that I had been accepted as a member of the team. I also felt I had gotten used to the clerkship, so I began to make an effort to grasp the whole team (around 10 patients), not only my assigned patients. In the final week, going beyond hematology/oncology, I was allowed to work like an intern at a general pediatric clinic that does primary care, and to observe an operation by Dr. 福島, a neurosurgeon who is a source of pride for Duke University and for Japan, and so, with real gratitude, I was able to enjoy Duke University to my heart's content, as I pleased. On holidays I played around Durham with four exchange students from Taiwan, enjoyed my hobby of piano at a music library three minutes' walk from my homestay, and was taken to a movie theater and an amusement park by 服部, who was studying abroad at UNC, and his roommate Albert. I was also happy that there were always local students rotating through the same department, who not only supported me in the clerkship but also stimulated me greatly with their active and hungry attitude. In the morning and at noon there were conferences for the pediatric residents as a whole, and being able to chat noisily with many medical students there was a very enjoyable time. The three areas called the North Carolina Triangle, Raleigh, Durham and Chapel Hill, were rich in nature, safe, and full of kind people, a very good place to live. My host family, who do research at Duke, not only cooked dinners for me but took me to the pottery class and baseball games that are the hobbies of the two of them, and treated me very kindly. The heartwarming life I spent with their two lovely dogs is a lifelong treasure to me.

[Life at McGill University] Because one month of clinical clerkship at Duke was not enough for me, I also did a clerkship at McGill University in Montreal, Canada. In Quebec, where Montreal is located, French is the official language for historical reasons. Canada is a nation of immigrants, but in Quebec, immigrants whose parents' native language is not English must all go to French-language schools, and English is not part of compulsory education. At first I was bewildered by a world of "Bonjour" beyond my imagination, but a third of the patients spoke English fluently, medical staff used only English with each other, and because French is dominant I had almost no inconvenience at the hospital. I was assigned to the emergency department of St. Mary Hospital, a McGill-affiliated hospital. The clerkship there was truly ultra-participatory and practical, and rather than a clinical clerkship I was steeped each day in a sense of fulfillment, thinking, "Ah, I'm really working." St. Mary Hospital is positioned as Montreal's community hospital, with 10 beds for walk-ins and 30 for ambulances, a hospital that puts quite a lot of weight on emergency care. The staff of the emergency department all work in shifts, taking a total of 15 shifts in four weeks of day shift (7:30-16:00), evening shift (16:00-24:00) and night shift (24:00-8:00). Seeing residents and attendings working in the same way, I keenly felt that the working environment in Japan is not a favorable one. For the clerkship content, I looked at patient information from the nurse, did the first touch (history and physical examination) alone, and summarized the information in the chart. Because the nurses sometimes took blood tests and ECGs beforehand, I summarized those too. Then I wrote the Assessment and Plan, presented them to the attending, discussed, and went to see the patient together again, repeating this for about six cases a day. Race, age and disease were wide-ranging, as befits a community hospital in the immigrant nation of Canada, and my impression was that it was really the practice of USMLE Step 2 CS. As in the United States, in Canada too, I felt that a big educational difference was that even medical students had to think through to treatment. Giving an opinion on a senior doctor's treatment policy is unthinkable in the clinical clerkships in Japan. I really struggled to think instantly and accurately about what tests to do and what treatment to give for the patient in trouble in front of me. Although I think I improved considerably thanks to the feedback the attending gave every time, I could not reach the level of the local students. Also, because I had never practiced writing charts, I was troubled by medical English, especially how to describe physical findings. But by the third month of studying abroad, I, who had been weak at English, could understand what patients were saying and say what I wanted to say fluently. I was very moved by that growth in myself. During my stay in Montreal, something very shocking also happened. A person died at my homestay. The cause was heroin poisoning. Around 3 a.m., the person injected themselves, fell asleep, and went into cardiac arrest. CPR was done, but in vain, and they passed away. What is burned vividly into my mind is the 15-year-old son, who was raging in shock at seeing a person die in front of him, saying "This is the reality around here." He apparently had also been taking heroin there. It was a moment when I witnessed that illegal drugs overseas are truly a familiar problem. I had never imagined that I would learn in this way how frightening drugs are and how serious and familiar the problem of abuse is, and I spent a sleepless night in strong shock. For now, "Canada is different from Japan" may be true, for better or for worse. But at least here, "this is the reality." I felt I must keep in mind that it is an environment in which even children can easily get drugs, and that this is not a problem being played out in a distant world.

[After the Study Abroad] Until I entered Nagoya University, I was neither good at English nor so fond of it. But when I learned of this study abroad program, I strongly wanted to study in the United States, and I steadily studied, adding short-term study abroad as well. When my plan was approved, I was truly overcome with emotion: I, who could not speak English at all until I entered Nagoya University, could study abroad in North America for three months! And through studying abroad my English improved a little more and my confidence gradually grew. I was also greatly stimulated from overseas, and I am very glad to have friends all over the world. But that was not all I gained from studying abroad. I feel that I, a negative thinker and a bundle of inferiority complexes, became a little mentally stronger and able to be positive about myself. "The world I have not yet seen is big. The self I have not yet seen is even bigger." I strongly felt the significance of studying abroad. Finally, the keywords I value as my own axis are "abundance, family, influence." I would be more than happy if my study abroad did not end within myself but influenced someone, and I think I want to connect it to the next chance without ending here.
